passage:
Charu: Lavanya, got a minute after your shift?
Lavanya: sure. is something wrong?
Charu: nothing you did. I've just noticed you've had four very hard families back to back this month
Lavanya: it's the job
Charu: it is. but you were in tears in the file room yesterday, and today you told Mrs Pinto "that's not my problem"
Lavanya: …I didn't mean it like that
Charu: I know. that's why I'm messaging. that's not you, that's tiredness
Lavanya: honestly I don't know what's happening to me
Charu: here's the plan: you're off Friday and Monday. Deepak takes your next two new cases. and we talk properly on Tuesday, with the staff counsellor if you want
Lavanya: are you sure the team can manage?
Charu: yes. the people who do the caring need looking after too. go home on time today
Lavanya: ok. thank you

qa.q: How many very hard families had Lavanya handled this month?
qa.a: Four very hard families back to back.

qa.q: What is Lavanya feeling in "I don't know what's happening to me"?
qa.a: Lavanya seems confused and a little frightened by the tears and sharpness, not recognising them as exhaustion.

qa.q: Which part of Charu's plan might help most, and why?
qa.a: Handing Lavanya's next two cases to Deepak shares the load straight away, while the days off and Tuesday's talk give rest and support.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pinto have felt being told "that's not my problem"?
qa.a: Mrs Pinto may have felt brushed off and hurt, which shows why a worn-out carer needs a break for everyone's sake.

grounding: A supervisor notices a caseworker turning tearful and sharp after back-to-back hard cases, and arranges days off, shared cases and a talk.

passage: Dr Sabina had run the primary health centre at Morigaon for two years, and she knew her staff. Bhupen, the male nurse, used to hum while dressing wounds and remember every child's name. But after the flood season, after the drowned fisherman and the baby they couldn't save, he changed. He stopped humming. He spoke to patients in short, hard sentences. On Thursday she found him behind the storeroom, eyes red, saying it was dust. Sabina didn't argue. That evening she changed the duty chart: two days off for Bhupen, his night shifts split between her and the pharmacist. Then she sat with him on the verandah with tea and asked, 'Tell me about the flood weeks.' He talked until it was dark.

qa.q: How long had Dr Sabina run the primary health centre?
qa.a: Two years.

qa.q: What might Bhupen's short, hard sentences and red eyes suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Bhupen is worn down and grieving after the hard cases of the flood season, not that he has stopped caring.

qa.q: What did Dr Sabina choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: She gave Bhupen days off, shared out his night shifts, and invited him to talk over tea, giving rest, a lighter load and someone to listen.

qa.q: How might the patients have noticed the change in Bhupen?
qa.a: Patients who knew his humming and warmth may have felt the hard sentences and wondered what had changed.

grounding: A health centre doctor sees a nurse grow hard and tearful after the flood season and arranges rest, shared shifts and a talk.

passage: At the care home in Alexandria, Dalia, the head nurse, noticed first that Siddiq had stopped joking. He had lost three residents in one month, including Mr Fawzi, whom he'd shaved every morning for two years. Now he moved through the rooms quickly, eyes down. Twice she'd seen him snap at the kitchen staff. On Tuesday she found him in the laundry, folding the same towel over and over, crying without a sound. She didn't make a speech. She rearranged the week: Siddiq on day shifts only, the hardest rooms shared with Nadia and Karim, and time with the home's counsellor on Thursday. Then she put a hand on his shoulder. 'You loved them well. Now let us look after you a little.'

qa.q: Whom had Siddiq shaved every morning for two years?
qa.a: Mr Fawzi.

qa.q: What does Siddiq folding the same towel over and over suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Siddiq is overwhelmed with grief and exhaustion after losing three residents, barely holding together.

qa.q: Why was Dalia's choice to rearrange the week better than giving a speech?
qa.a: Day shifts, shared rooms and a counsellor session gave Siddiq real rest and support, which words alone couldn't.

qa.q: How might Nadia and Karim feel about taking on the hardest rooms?
qa.a: They may feel the extra weight but also understand, knowing Siddiq has carried a lot, and may trust they'd get the same care one day.

grounding: A head nurse sees a caregiver grow sharp and tearful after several deaths and arranges lighter shifts, a shared load and counselling.

passage:
At the children's shelter home in Nagpur, Shankar, the superintendent, liked to walk the corridors after dinner. For two years the loudest room had been Lokesh's: Lokesh, the house-father, playing carrom with the boys, laughing at his own bad shots.
Since the monsoon, three boys had arrived in one month, each with a story that made the staff go silent. Shankar noticed the carrom board stayed under the bed. Lokesh shouted at a boy for a dropped plate. On Friday Shankar found him in the storeroom, sorting blankets, eyes wet, pretending it was dust.
Shankar didn't lecture. He shut the door and said, "You've taken the heaviest three this month. Sit with me." They drank tea on the sacks of rice. Then Shankar changed the roster: two days off for Lokesh, the night duty split with Venkat, and a talk with the visiting counsellor on Tuesday. "The boys need you," he said. "So I need you rested."

qa.q: Where did Shankar find Lokesh on Friday?
qa.a: In the storeroom, sorting blankets.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling when he pretended his wet eyes were from dust?
qa.a: He was probably worn down and sad from the boys' stories, and a little embarrassed to be seen crying at work.

qa.q: Which of Shankar's choices mattered most for Lokesh, and why?
qa.a: Changing the roster for rest, sharing the night duty and arranging a counsellor mattered most, because it lightened the load instead of only offering kind words.

qa.q: How might the boys at the shelter be affected by Lokesh getting rest?
qa.a: They may get back the laughing house-father who played carrom, instead of an adult who shouts over a dropped plate.

grounding: It shows a supervisor noticing a caregiver becoming hard and tearful after too many hard cases and arranging rest, talk and shared load.

passage:
Subject: Your next two weeks

Hi Shankar,
I want to say this in writing so you know it's not a passing comment.
You took four overnight calls on the helpline last week, including the long one on Friday that you stayed on till the police arrived. You handled it beautifully. But in Sunday's debrief you didn't speak once, and on Monday you told a new volunteer, "Just follow the script, feelings don't help." That isn't the calm young man who trained with me.
So, three things. I've taken you off nights until the 20th. Pooja will pair with you on day shifts so no hard call is yours alone. And let's have chai on Thursday at five, just to talk, nothing formal. If you'd like, the counsellor we use for volunteers keeps Saturday slots.
You carry other people's worst nights for them. Someone has to carry a bit of yours too.
Lokesh
Volunteer coordinator

qa.q: Until when has Lokesh taken Shankar off nights?
qa.a: Until the 20th.

qa.q: What worried Lokesh about Shankar's comment to the new volunteer?
qa.a: Lokesh was worried because the comment sounded hard and unlike the caring young man Lokesh had trained, a sign that the heavy calls were wearing Shankar down.

qa.q: Which of Lokesh's steps would help Shankar most, and why?
qa.a: Pairing Shankar with Pooja so no hard call is carried alone may help most, because it shares the weight while the rest from nights lets him recover.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel reading this email?
qa.a: He might feel caught out at first, then relieved and cared for, since someone noticed his silence and acted instead of just praising his work.

grounding: It shows a coordinator who notices a helpline volunteer growing hard after many difficult calls and arranges rest, a talk and a shared load.

passage:
You asked me for this interview how I noticed Afreen was burning out. I'm Deepika, and I run the home-care team for older patients here.
Afreen was our warmest carer. She'd sing to patients, remember their grandchildren's names. Then, last winter, three of her patients died in six weeks.
I started noticing small things. She stopped singing. She'd snap at the driver. Once I found her crying in the van, and when I asked, she said, "I'm fine, it's just the cold."
Another day she said, flat as a wall, "They all die anyway."
That's when I knew. I gave her a week off, paid. I sat with her for an hour and just listened. When she came back, I split her cases with two others and started a Friday tea where the whole team talks about hard days.
Caring people need someone caring for them too.

qa.q: How many of Afreen's patients died in six weeks?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Deepika thinking when Afreen said "They all die anyway"?
qa.a: Deepika felt alarmed and concerned, realising Afreen was burning out after too many hard losses.

qa.q: Which of Deepika's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: A paid week off, an hour of listening, shared cases and a Friday tea helped, because they gave Afreen rest, talk and a lighter load.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Deepika sat and listened?
qa.a: She probably felt seen and relieved, having someone notice her pain instead of just the work.

grounding: It shows a supervisor noticing a caregiver grow hard and tearful after too many deaths and arranging rest, talk and shared load.

passage:
I'm Anirban, the shift supervisor at the care home. I want to write down what I saw with Lakshmi this month.
Lakshmi has been here four years, always first to hold a resident's hand. In October we had a hard stretch: two residents in hospital, one fall, a family complaint.
I noticed she stopped taking her tea break. Her voice got clipped. On Tuesday, a resident spilt her soup and Lakshmi said, "Again?", sharp, and then went into the store room. When she came out, her eyes were red.
I can't know exactly what she was feeling. But I've seen this before.
That evening I asked her to sit with me. I said, "You've had a heavy month." She cried for a while. I gave her three days off, swapped her with Ravi on the night rota, and we're starting a short weekly team talk.

qa.q: How long has Lakshmi worked at the care home?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: What was Anirban thinking after seeing Lakshmi's red eyes?
qa.a: Anirban felt concerned, recognising signs of burnout while admitting uncertainty about exactly what she felt.

qa.q: What steps did Anirban take, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Anirban listened, gave three days off, changed the rota and started a weekly team talk, giving Lakshmi rest, talk and shared load.

qa.q: How might the resident who spilt soup have felt when Lakshmi snapped?
qa.a: The resident may have felt hurt or embarrassed, not knowing Lakshmi was exhausted.

grounding: It shows a supervisor observing a caregiver grow sharp and tearful after hard cases and arranging rest, talk and shared load.

passage:
Monday. Gargi, twenty-six, team lead at the children's shelter, noticed Farida sitting alone in the courtyard at lunch, eyes shut. Farida had handled three emergency admissions that week. Gargi made a note to check in.
Thursday. A boy threw a plate. Farida, usually so patient, shouted at him, then stood trembling in the corridor. Gargi saw her wipe her face quickly when she noticed Gargi watching.
That afternoon Gargi called her into the office, closed the door and asked, "How are you, really?" Farida cried and said she dreamt about the children every night.
Next Monday. Farida was on two days' leave. Her admissions were split between Gargi and another worker. On Wednesday there'd be a new team meeting: one hour every week to talk about hard cases.

qa.q: How many emergency admissions had Farida handled that week?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Gargi thinking when she saw Farida trembling in the corridor?
qa.a: Gargi felt worried and protective, seeing that Farida's patience was breaking after too many hard cases.

qa.q: Which of Gargi's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking privately how Farida really was, giving leave, sharing her admissions and setting up a weekly talk helped, because caring staff need rest and support too.

qa.q: How might the boy who threw the plate have felt when Farida shouted?
qa.a: He might have felt scared or more upset, since Farida was usually so patient.

grounding: It shows a team lead noticing a caregiver's burnout over days and arranging rest, talk and shared load.

passage:
"Manoj, you're new in charge of the night nurses, so let me tell you about my first year as a ward supervisor. I, Santosh, was a young man of twenty-five, younger than half my staff.
There was a nurse, Mary, gentle as anything. One monsoon we had case after case of children with fever. I noticed Mary stopped chatting at tea. Then one day she answered a worried father very sharply. That evening I found her crying in the linen room.
I could have written her up. Instead I sat with her and asked what she was carrying. She said, 'Every child's face.'
I gave her two lighter weeks, moved one of the hard cases to myself, and started a ten-minute talk at shift change for everyone. She stayed on the ward twenty years. Carers break quietly, beta. Watch for it."

qa.q: Where did Santosh find Mary crying?
qa.a: He found her crying in the linen room.

qa.q: What did young Santosh feel when he found Mary in the linen room, and why?
qa.a: He felt concern and care rather than anger, seeing that her sharpness came from being worn down by case after case.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for Mary?
qa.a: Santosh chose to sit with her instead of writing her up, then gave her lighter weeks, took on a hard case himself, and started shift-change talks.

qa.q: What was it like for Mary during that monsoon of fever cases?
qa.a: She was carrying every child's face and grew quiet, sharp and tearful, worn down by too much sorrow.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing a caring nurse grow sharp and tearful after many hard cases, and arranging rest, talk and shared work.

passage:
The care home in Nashik was two staff short all week, and Pradeep, the young shift supervisor, had no one spare to call in. On Friday he noticed Irawati, usually the one who sang to the residents, feeding Mrs Joshi without a word, her jaw tight.
Later he found her in the store room, eyes wet, folding the same towel over and over. "Sorry, sir. It's nothing. Two of my ladies died this month."
Pradeep sat on an upturned crate. "It's not nothing. You've been doing the work of two."
He could not give her the week off with no cover. So he took her difficult evening rounds himself, swapped her to the day shift, and arranged a call with the home's counsellor for Monday. "Talk to me every day this week," he said.

qa.q: How many staff short was the care home that week?
qa.a: The care home was two staff short all week.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel when he found Irawati in the store room?
qa.a: He felt concerned and caring; he did not dismiss her tears as nothing, because he could see how worn down she was.

qa.q: How did Pradeep support Irawati even without spare staff?
qa.a: He took her difficult evening rounds himself, moved her to day shift, arranged a counsellor call and asked her to talk to him daily.

qa.q: What is it like for Irawati when two of her residents die in a month?
qa.a: She is grieving and exhausted, losing her usual warmth and struggling to keep going.

grounding: A supervisor notices a carer grow tight-jawed and tearful after hard losses and arranges shared load, talk and rest despite a staff shortage.

passage:
Trisha had supervised the child helpline team in Kolkata for only four months, but she knew each counsellor's voice. On Wednesday she realised Chetan, who usually joked between calls, had not spoken in two hours. His replies to callers were correct, but flat. Twice he hung up and sat very still with his headset on.
After the shift she asked him to walk with her to the tea stall downstairs. "You took three hard cases in a row yesterday," she said. "How are you really?"
Chetan looked at the traffic. "I keep hearing the last kid. I feel stone."
Trisha nodded. "Then you've been carrying too much alone." She put him on lighter calls for the week, set up a debrief with the team on Friday, and told him to take Thursday off.

qa.q: Where did Trisha take Chetan after the shift?
qa.a: She asked him to walk with her to the tea stall downstairs.

qa.q: What made Trisha worried about Chetan?
qa.a: She was concerned because Chetan, who usually joked, had been silent for two hours, flat with callers, and sitting very still after hanging up.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's steps could help a caring team last longer?
qa.a: Lighter calls for the week, a team debrief on Friday and a day off, so the hard feelings are shared and rested instead of carried alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Chetan after three hard cases in a row?
qa.a: He keeps hearing the last child and feels like stone, numb and worn down by the heaviness.

grounding: A supervisor notices a counsellor go quiet and flat after many hard calls and arranges rest, talk and shared load.

passage:
'Jaya, you've been on the paediatric ward how long now?'
'Eight months, Rekha Ma'am.'
'I saw you in the sluice room yesterday. Crying.'
'I'm fine. Just tired.'
'And on Monday you snapped at the new trainee over a thermometer.'
Jaya looked at the floor. 'I'm sorry. I don't know what's happening to me. I used to love this.'
'You've had four very hard cases in two weeks. That changes anyone.'
'So I'm not bad at this?'
'You're good at this. That's why it's hurting.' Rekha pulled out the rota. 'You're off Friday and Saturday. Next week you'll share the heavy cases with Anu. And Thursday, you and I will have tea and talk properly.'
Jaya's eyes filled. 'Thank you.'

qa.q: How long had Jaya been on the paediatric ward?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What might Rekha have felt on seeing Jaya crying in the sluice room?
qa.a: Rekha was probably concerned and protective, recognising the signs of a caregiver worn down.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's steps could other supervisors copy?
qa.a: Naming what she noticed kindly, giving time off, sharing the heavy cases and setting a time to talk.

qa.q: How does Jaya feel after Rekha's plan?
qa.a: Jaya feels relieved and grateful, her eyes filling, after fearing she was bad at her job.

grounding: A supervisor sees a nurse grow tearful and sharp after too many hard cases and arranges rest, talk and a shared load.

passage: I noticed it first in Alka's eyes. I'm Noor, and I run the counselling team at a women's shelter in Bhopal. Alka is one of our best counsellors: patient, warm, funny. But after the winter, when we had three very difficult cases in a row, she changed. She stopped laughing at lunch. She was short with the receptionist. One afternoon I found her sitting in her car, not moving. She said, 'I don't feel anything anymore. Is that bad?' I told her no. I told her it's what happens when caring people carry too much for too long. We made a plan together: two weeks of lighter cases, a weekly session with an outside supervisor, and Friday afternoons off. I checked in every few days. By March, Alka was laughing at lunch again.

qa.q: Where does Noor run the counselling team?
qa.a: At a women's shelter in Bhopal.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on finding Alka sitting in her car?
qa.a: Noor felt concerned and protective, seeing a warm colleague worn down by too many hard cases.

qa.q: What made Noor's plan effective?
qa.a: It reduced Alka's load, added outside supervision and time off, and included regular check-ins, so care for the carer was ongoing.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt hearing Noor say it wasn't bad?
qa.a: Alka probably felt relieved and less ashamed, understanding that the numbness came from caring too much.

grounding: A supervisor notices a counsellor grow flat and short after too many hard cases and arranges rest, supervision and a lighter load.

passage:
Ward supervisor's note, old-age home, Mysuru

Over the past month I have watched Aparna, one of our kindest care workers, change. We lost three residents in five weeks, and she sat with each of them at the end. Since then she has been short with the families, cried in the store room twice, and on Tuesday told Mahima, 'I don't know why I bother.' This is not the Aparna we know. It is a caring person who has carried too much. Today I sat with her and said so. Next steps: she will have three days' leave this week, Mahima will share her residents for a fortnight, and I have booked her a session with the counsellor who visits on Thursdays. I will check in with her every Monday.

Sister Leela, supervisor

qa.q: How many residents had died in five weeks?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What does Sister Leela seem to feel about the change in Aparna?
qa.a: Sister Leela seems concerned and caring, seeing it as the strain of a kind person carrying too much.

qa.q: Which steps in the plan share the load?
qa.a: Three days' leave, Mahima sharing her residents for a fortnight, a counsellor's session and weekly check-ins.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel hearing Aparna say 'I don't know why I bother'?
qa.a: Mahima might have felt worried and surprised, since it didn't sound like Aparna.

grounding: A supervisor sees a care worker grow hard and tearful after losing several residents and arranges rest, talk and a shared load.

passage:
Tuesday night
Manjula snapped at the new volunteer today, over a misfiled form. Manjula, who once sat with Mrs D'Souza for three hours just holding her hand. After her fourth home visit this week to a family losing someone, she came back and sat in the van with wet eyes, not moving. When I asked, she said, "I'm fine, just tired," and then laughed too hard at nothing.
Afreen, you're her supervisor, I told myself. I should have seen it coming; I kept giving her the hardest cases because she's the best at them.
So: I've moved two of her visits next week to Rohan and me, and she's off on Friday, no arguments. We're having chai tomorrow, just to talk. Caring people need someone caring for them too. That includes me, probably.

qa.q: How many of Manjula's visits were moved next week?
qa.a: Two of her visits, moved to Rohan and Afreen.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling after noticing the changes in Manjula?
qa.a: Afreen feels concerned and a little guilty, having kept giving Manjula the hardest cases because she was the best at them.

qa.q: What steps did Afreen take, and why do they fit?
qa.a: Sharing the load by moving two visits, giving Friday off and setting up a chai talk; together they give Manjula rest, company and less weight to carry.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel about being given Friday off?
qa.a: Manjula might protest at first, but likely feels relieved and cared for, since she has been worn down and tearful.

grounding: A supervisor notices a caregiver growing hard and tearful after hard cases and arranges rest, talk and a shared load.
